title: Multi-cycle iterative divider + single 33x33 multiplier: take DIV/REM off the EX critical path
motivation:
Fmax is 5.44 MHz because the worst path (199.8 ns, 156 cells) runs
forward_unit -> ex_stage operand mux -> alu -> EX/MEM register through the
purely combinational 32-bit `/` and `%` operators in alu.sv (four of them:
signed/unsigned quotient and remainder). Everything else in the 5-stage
pipeline is an order of magnitude shorter. CoreMark executes almost no
DIV/REM instructions, so the whole clock period is being set by an
operation that is practically never used. The same alu.sv also builds three
separate 64x64-bit multipliers (mul_ss, mul_uu, mul_su with 64-bit
sign-extended operands) where one 33x33 signed multiplier is sufficient;
once the divider is gone those become the next-longest EX path and they
also waste DSP blocks / LUTs (12.3k LUT4 today vs. a 10k target).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational divider with a sequential radix-2 restoring
divider that iterates one quotient bit per clock while the pipeline is
stalled, and collapse the three multipliers into one.

Divider (new rtl/divider.sv, instantiated in ex_stage):
  - Start when ID/EX holds a valid DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU and the unit is idle.
    On the start cycle latch the *forwarded* rs1/rs2 (and op), because the
    EX/MEM and MEM/WB forwarding sources drain away while EX is held; the
    latched values also feed EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val/write_data for RVFI.
  - Work on magnitudes: take |a|, |b| for DIV/REM, run 32 shift-subtract
    steps on a {remainder, quotient} shift register with one 33-bit
    subtractor, then conditionally negate (quotient if signs differ and
    b != 0; remainder if dividend negative). This yields the RV32M corner
    cases for free: x/0 -> all-ones quotient, remainder = dividend;
    INT_MIN/-1 -> INT_MIN, remainder 0. ~34-35 cycles per divide.
  - `div_busy` = valid div in ID/EX and result not yet done. While busy:
    hazard_unit holds PC and ID/EX (stall_if/stall_id) and ex_stage writes
    a bubble (valid=0, reg_write=0, mem_read=mem_write=0) into EX/MEM
    unless dmem_stall is already holding EX/MEM. On the done cycle (and
    only when EX/MEM is not held by dmem_stall) the instruction advances
    with the divider result as alu_result; the FSM returns to idle exactly
    when the instruction leaves EX. A redirect cannot originate from a
    divide in EX, and a flush of ID/EX (reset) must reset the FSM.
  - Under `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` the unit keeps the identical
    start/busy/done handshake but returns the ALTOPS formula
    ((a - b) ^ const) after a short fixed latency (1-2 cycles), so the
    BMC depth budget and the liveness check still close while formal
    proves the stall/forward/bubble behaviour of the new handshake.

Multiplier (rtl/alu.sv): build one signed 33x33 product
  p = $signed({a_sx, a}) * $signed({b_sx, b})   (66 bits)
with a_sx = a[31] for MULH/MULHSU else 0 and b_sx = b[31] for MULH else 0;
MUL = p[31:0], MULH/MULHU/MULHSU = p[63:32]. Same results, one third of
the multiplier hardware, shorter EX path. MUL stays single-cycle so the
multiply-heavy CoreMark matrix kernel loses no IPC.

The divider case arms are removed from the combinational ALU case
statement; alu.sv keeps ALTOPS and real branches consistent.

Expected result: iterations/cycle unchanged to within <1% (DIV/REM are
vanishingly rare in CoreMark, each now costs ~34 extra cycles), while the
critical path drops from ~200 ns to the forward-mux -> multiplier/adder ->
EX/MEM path (a few tens of ns at worst), i.e. Fmax rises several-fold.
The real gain is expected to be far above the +50% schema ceiling.

Measured during hypothesis generation (Gowin flow, place option 0, scratch
copy of the RTL with the DIV/REM arms deleted and the single 33x33
multiplier in place, MUL still single-cycle): Fmax 49.41 MHz vs 5.44 MHz,
logic 1971 LUT (was 12312), 2 DSP. Deleting the multiplier as well gave
46.7 MHz, i.e. the single-cycle multiplier is NOT the next bottleneck, so
MUL must stay single-cycle (no IPC loss). The remaining worst path
(~25.5 ns) is regfile/forward -> EX branch resolve -> redirect ->
hazard/flush -> ID/EX, untouched by this change. Keep the divider's
start/busy logic off that path: derive div_busy from registered ID/EX
ctrl bits and the divider's own FSM state only.

lesson: - 2026-11-23 hyp-20261123-001-r1s0 (regression, +748.76%): Replacing the combinational `/`/`%` in alu.sv with a stalled multi-cycle radix-2 divider passed all gates and alone gave ~8.5x (that divider was the whole ~200 ns period), yet it lost the round to sibling hyp-20261123-002-r1s1 (+1039%), which did the same plus the two things this one deliberately left alone — registering the 33x33 multiplier (MUL +1 cycle) and taking `redirect` off the if_stage NOP mux -> load-use compare -> ID/EX-enable path (not measured separately); the probe conclusion "deleting the multiplier doesn't raise Fmax, so MUL is not the next bottleneck" was a misread, because once the dominant path is gone the remaining ~25 ns EX paths are co-critical and mask each other, so a single-seed delete-one-block probe can't rank them and they have to be cut together.

title: Multi-cycle M-unit: iterative divider + registered DSP multiplier behind an EX-stall handshake
motivation:
Fmax is 5.44 MHz because the worst path (199.8 ns, 150 logic levels) runs
MEM/WB.rd -> forward_unit -> EX operand mux -> alu.sv combinational 32-bit
`/` and `%` -> EX/MEM.alu_result (= dmem BSRAM address). The single-cycle
dividers are also why the core is 12.3k LUT4 with only 460 FFs. Three
separate 64-bit combinational multipliers (mul_ss/mul_uu/mul_su, 6 DSPs)
sit in the same forward -> ALU -> EX/MEM loop and are the next limiter once
the divider is gone. CoreMark's timed region executes essentially no
divides and only a few percent multiplies, so making these ops multi-cycle
costs ~1-3% cycles (CoreMark/MHz stays ~2.15-2.2) while the clock period
can drop by an order of magnitude. Nothing else in the design is within
10x of this path, so every other optimisation is invisible until this
structural change lands.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Take multiply/divide out of the single-cycle EX path. A new sequential
M-unit (rtl/muldiv.sv) executes them over several cycles while the M
instruction waits in ID/EX; EX/MEM receives bubbles until the result is
registered. All RV32I ops stay single-cycle, so the EX loop becomes
forward-mux -> 32-bit add/shift/compare -> EX/MEM.

Measured evidence (Gowin P&R, place option 0, throwaway copies of rtl/):
  - DIV/REM arms stubbed, combinational multiplier kept: Fmax 49.1 MHz,
    2071 LUT4 (was 12312). Two co-critical paths at ~25.6 ns:
    (a) regfile -> fwd mux -> multiplier (DSP) -> EX/MEM/dmem address;
    (b) regfile -> fwd mux -> branch compare -> redirect -> if_stage NOP
        mux -> hazard_unit load-use compare -> ID/EX enable.
  - DIV/REM and MUL arms stubbed: 43.8 MHz (same path (b), P&R noise).
So this change alone is worth ~45-50 MHz = fitness ~100-110 iter/s (~9x,
far beyond the +50% the schema field can express); registering the
multiplier removes (a) and item 6 below shortens (b).

Design contract for the implementer:
1. muldiv.sv, ports: clock, reset, start, op, a, b -> busy/done, result.
   - Divider: radix-2 restoring, 1 bit/cycle on magnitudes (setup cycle
     takes |a|,|b| and records signs; 32 iterate cycles of a 33-bit
     subtract + shift; final cycle applies sign fix into result_q).
     RV32M corner cases fall out of the algorithm with one rule: negate
     the quotient only if signs differ AND b != 0 (div-by-0 -> all ones,
     rem-by-0 -> dividend, INT_MIN/-1 -> INT_MIN, rem 0). No early-out
     needed: divides are not on CoreMark's timed path.
   - Multiplier: ONE 33x33 signed multiply (operand sign bits =
     a[31]&a_signed, b[31]&b_signed) replacing the three 64-bit ones.
     Operands are registered (DSP input regs), product registered
     (DSP output reg), result_q = op==MUL ? p[31:0] : p[63:32].
     Start with 2 extra cycles; cut to 1 extra cycle only if
     `make timing` shows reg -> DSP -> EX/MEM is not the worst path.
   - Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` keep the SAME FSM/handshake but
     compute the ALTOPS formulas from the captured operands with a fixed
     2-cycle latency. Required: insn checks are 20-step BMC and liveness
     allows ~10 cycles between retirements, so a 34-cycle divide cannot
     retire inside the window. Real latency is covered by cosim + cocotb.
2. ex_stage.sv: m_op = in.valid && ctrl.is_muldiv (new decoded ctrl bit so
   EX does not compare alu_op). start = m_op && FSM idle, operands = the
   post-forward rs1/rs2. ex_busy = m_op && !done. When done, EX/MEM
   captures result_q through the existing alu_result mux; the FSM returns
   to idle on the cycle EX/MEM actually captures (!stall_ex_mem).
3. hazard_unit.sv: stall_if |= ex_busy; stall_id |= ex_busy; new output
   bubble_ex_mem = ex_busy && !dmem_stall (EX/MEM <= '0). dmem_stall keeps
   priority (EX/MEM holds, M-unit keeps iterating or waits in DONE). An
   M-op in EX is never a load or branch, so load_use/redirect/flush_id
   cannot fire against it.
4. Operand staleness (the classic bug): while the M-op waits in EX its
   producers drain out of EX/MEM and MEM/WB, so ID/EX.rs?_val would be
   stale at the done cycle (wrong rvfi_rs?_rdata, and wrong operands if
   start were late). Fix in id_stage.sv: whenever ID/EX holds (stall &&
   !flush) write the post-forward rs1/rs2 back into ID/EX.rs1_val/rs2_val.
   Forwarding is then correct on every held cycle by induction, and
   EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val are right when the M-op finally moves.
5. alu.sv keeps only RV32I ops (M arms deleted in both the ALTOPS and real
   branches, since both now live in muldiv.sv and must stay consistent).
6. Shorten co-critical path (b): redirect and load_use_hazard are mutually
   exclusive (both are functions of the SAME ID/EX instruction: redirect
   needs is_branch/is_jump, load-use needs mem_read), and on redirect
   flush_id already zeroes ID/EX with priority over stall. So if_stage
   must stop muxing the IF/ID instruction with NOP on `redirect`: keep the
   NOP mux for imem_stall only (imem_ready is a flop) and let redirect act
   only through flush_id and the PC mux. hazard_unit then sees raw
   instr[19:15]/[24:20] and redirect no longer feeds decode/regfile-read/
   load-use logic. out.valid may still be gated by redirect.
Invariants untouched: decoder legality, rvfi_order (+1 per valid MEM/WB),
trap discipline, top-level IO, nret=1.

lesson: - 2026-11-23 hyp-20261123-002-r1s1 (improvement, +1039.44%): Moving `*`, `/`, `%` out of alu.sv into a stalled multi-cycle muldiv.sv (ex_busy holds PC and ID/EX, EX/MEM takes bubbles) won entirely on clock period — Fmax 5.44 -> 63.3 MHz, 12312 -> 2381 LUT4, 6 -> 2 DSP — for only ~2% more CoreMark cycles (derived from fitness/Fmax, ~2.18 CoreMark/MHz), because the timed region runs almost no divides and few multiplies, so M-op latency is nearly free and MUL needs only DSP input registers (1 extra cycle; operand reg -> DSP -> EX/MEM was not in the top-5 paths of the implementer's single-seed timing run, so the product register was dropped); the design passed formal/cosim with a fixed 1-extra-cycle ALTOPS variant of the same FSM (a 35-cycle divide cannot retire inside the 20-step BMC) and with post-forward rs1/rs2 written back into ID/EX on every held cycle because the waiting op's producers drain out of EX/MEM and MEM/WB (the unrefreshed case was not tried), which is the template for any future op that waits in EX; the M-unit is now off the critical path, which sits at ~21-22 ns in two co-critical single-cycle EX loops (regfile -> operand mux -> branch compare -> redirect -> ID/EX flush, ~6 ns shorter than the sibling's 27.8 ns version that still ran through the if_stage NOP mux and hazard_unit load-use compare, a cross-design comparison; and MEM/WB.rd -> forward_unit -> ALU add -> dmem BSRAM address), so the next gains must come from branch resolution and forwarding, not from tuning the M-unit.

title: Fetch-cycle branch prediction: bimodal direction + in-cycle pc+imm target, zero-bubble taken branches and JALs
motivation:
The core has no branch prediction: every taken conditional branch, JAL and
JALR is resolved in EX and redirects the PC from there, killing the
instruction sitting in the merged IF/ID stage (one bubble per redirect).
Measured on this RTL (Verilator cosim, CoreMark with --istall --dstall,
first 3.0M cycles / 1.95M retirements, RVFI trace):
  CPI = 1.535; conditional branches = 18.1% of instructions, 55.6% taken;
  JAL = 1.69%, JALR = 0.47%.
  Redirects = 12.2% of instructions = 7.96% of ALL cycles are redirect
  bubbles.
This core has a property that makes prediction nearly free: there is NO
IF/ID register. The fetched word (io_imemData) is visible combinationally
in the same cycle the PC addresses it, so the branch/JAL target can be
computed from the instruction itself (pc + B/J-immediate) in the fetch
cycle and steered straight into the PC register. No BTB, no target
misprediction, and a correctly predicted taken branch costs ZERO bubbles.
Only the direction needs predicting.
Fmax (5.4 MHz) is set by the ~200 ns combinational divider path in EX, so
the new fetch-cycle path (imemData -> imm mux -> 32-bit add -> PC mux) and
the 1-LUT change to the EX redirect are an order of magnitude off the
critical path; the gain is pure iterations/cycle.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a decode-time (fetch-cycle) branch predictor to the merged IF/ID stage
and turn the EX redirect into a misprediction-only redirect.

1. Pre-decode in if_stage directly from imem_data: is_branch (opcode
   1100011), is_jal (1101111). Compute pred_target = pc + (is_jal ? J-imm :
   B-imm) with one dedicated 32-bit adder.
2. Direction: new branch_predictor.sv - 256-entry table of 2-bit saturating
   counters indexed by pc[9:2] (bimodal), async read at fetch, sync write
   from EX, no reset on the array (LUT-RAM friendly). JAL is always
   predicted taken.
     pred_taken = !(flush || redirect) && !imm[1]
                  && (is_jal || (is_branch && ctr[1]))
   Never predict taken when the target would be misaligned (imm[1]=1), so
   the existing misalign-trap behaviour (no redirect, pc_next = pc+4) is
   untouched.
3. PC update: EX redirect keeps top priority; else if !stall,
   pc <= pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4. pred_taken rides in the IF/ID
   bundle and is latched into ID/EX under the existing stall/flush rules,
   so the bit in ID/EX always equals what the PC really did (imem stall ->
   bundle is a NOP with pred_taken=0; load-use -> ID/EX flushed and PC
   held; dmem stall -> both held; redirect -> ID/EX flushed).
4. EX verify: actual_taken = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault.
   redirect = (actual_taken != pred_taken)   (JALR is never predicted, so
   it redirects exactly as today);
   redirect_target = actual_taken ? (is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target)
                                  : pc + 4.
   pc_next / trap / link-value logic is unchanged (always the
   architecturally correct next PC), so every prediction is verified and
   ANY predictor contents are functionally safe - formal needs no
   assumptions about table state, and riscv-formal pc_fwd/pc_bwd act as the
   safety net for the steering logic.
5. Training: when a valid conditional branch leaves EX (gated by
   !stall_ex_mem so a branch held by a dmem stall trains once), update the
   counter at in.pc[9:2] with the resolved direction. Only one instruction
   is ever speculative (the one in IF/ID while its predecessor is in EX),
   so no repair/checkpoint logic exists anywhere.

Trace-driven evaluation of exactly this scheme on the measured CoreMark
RVFI trace (counters initialised weakly-not-taken):
  static BTFN            20.6% mispredict -> +5.5% iterations/cycle
  bimodal 64             9.9%             -> +6.9%
  bimodal 256 (proposed) 8.45%            -> +7.1%
  bimodal 1024           7.6%             -> +7.25%
  gshare 256 (h=4..8)    8.8-10.7%        -> +6.8..7.1% (worse: aliasing)
  gshare 4096 h=12       6.4%             -> +7.4%
  + 4-entry RAS          99.9% of returns -> only +0.35% extra
Almost all of the gain comes from the zero-bubble in-cycle target, not from
predictor sophistication, so the proposal deliberately takes the simplest
point: bimodal-256, no global history, no RAS (rejected: +0.35% does not
justify a 30-bit predicted-target field in ID/EX plus a jalr-adder ->
comparator -> redirect path). Redirect bubbles drop from 12.2% to ~2.0% of
instructions (8.45% of branches + all JALRs): cycles per iteration fall
~6.7%, i.e. about +7% CoreMark iter/s at unchanged Fmax.

Async read port indexed by fetch pc[9:2] -> pred bit = ctr[1]; sync update port (en, pc index, taken) driven from EX. PC: redirect ? redirect_target : (!stall ? (pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4) : hold). Emit pred_taken in the IF/ID bundle; expose pc[9:2] lookup to the predictor.
Latch in.pred_taken into the ID/EX register (cleared on flush with the rest of the bundle, held on stall).

lesson: - 2026-11-23 hyp-20261123-003-r1s2 (regression, +9.49%): The fetch-cycle predictor worked as modelled and is a "regression" only because it lost the round to the sibling divider fix (+1039%) and was never merged — a ~7% IPC idea cannot win a round while one path makes the clock 10x too slow, so it must be re-proposed on the 63 MHz champion: a 256x2-bit bimodal LUT-RAM at pc[9:2], the target computed as pc + B/J-imm straight from `imem_data` in the merged IF/ID stage (no IF/ID register), and an EX redirect only when `actual_taken != pred_taken` cut CoreMark cycles 4,491,485 -> 4,193,173 (+7.11% iter/cycle, matching the RVFI-trace model's +7.1%; the other ~2.2% of the headline is placement noise, median Fmax 5.442 -> 5.564 MHz with the ~200 ns divider still the worst path) for 16 LUT-RAM cells + 3 FFs, and riscv-formal passed 53/53 with the table unconstrained because every prediction is checked in EX against the architectural next PC; the same ~298k saved redirect bubbles should be worth about +7% on the champion's 4.585M cycles (not re-measured), but "free on timing" was only shown behind the divider — on the champion the `!= pred_taken` XOR, the extra pc+4 arm of `redirect_target`, and this version's `flush || redirect` kill in if_stage (the very term the champion removed) all land on the now-critical regfile -> branch compare -> redirect loop, where ~1.1 ns on the 15.8 ns period cancels the whole gain.
